research_concepts: role portability or transfer across contexts
methodological_questions: Can a cut-share versus drive-share contrast in shapers be tested with 24 units at useful power?
Is the cut/drive classification reliable and validated when derived from play-by-play play types?
Do earlier portability studies with different units and populations support transferring their conclusions to shapers and role transfer?
Which confounders (usage, minutes, lineup, teammate and opponent quality, sample exposure in playoffs) must be controlled in a role-transfer comparison?
How many role-share contrasts are being examined, and how is multiplicity controlled?

historical_evidence.finding: Studied cut- vs drive-based connector portability in n=92 connector movers. Pre-move cut share predicted whether organizational function reproduced after a move (cut share rho=+0.265, p=0.011, AUC 0.653; cut-drive rho=+0.314, p=0.002; drive rho=-0.278, p=0.007). Top cut tercile was 65% portable (median Delta +0.167) versus 35% in the bottom tercile (median Delta -0.039). LOO AUC 0.622; permutation p=0.005 from 5000 label shuffles. Record notes sample and power limitation (SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER) and a small-sample limit. Full text was not retrieved; the record is truncated.

Tested whether diet-matching to a destination's thin initiation jobs predicts better post-move outcomes. Taxonomy connector subset had n=19 (delta match vs mismatch median +0.540 vs +0.069, p=0.156). Travel-check delta p=0.413. An all-movers binary delta gave p=0.0283 (n=198), but the continuous Spearman was -0.034 (p recorded as 0), so the binary result did not replicate and was not the licensed connector test.

Compared observed DRIVE H2 PPP with feasibility-constrained baselines in n=44. Gap to baseline B_game was -0.058 (p=0.6069); gap to B_fixed was -0.066 (p=0.2175); gap to coach default was +0.043 (p=0.3052). MDE at 80% power was about 0.180 PPP (SD about 0.34), or 0.265 if SD is about 0.5.

Archived check of whether portability relates to destination net-rating change for movers. Recorded only as 'underpowered and null once corrected for landing-spot quality' with no numbers; sample size not recorded. Dropped from Paper 1.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Binary diet-match test on all movers, and taxonomy-connector subset test of diet-matching to destination structural gaps.
failed_approaches.why: Connector subsets were n=19 (and n=40 in the note), too small for the test. The all-movers binary p=0.0283 did not replicate under the continuous Spearman (-0.034), so it was not a robust finding. Recorded as untestable with a small-sample limit.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Comparison of observed DRIVE-as-best PPP against constrained baselines.
failed_approaches.why: n=44 gave an MDE of about 0.18 PPP, larger than the observed gap of -0.066, so a true null cannot be separated from an effect up to 0.18 PPP. Recorded as low-power, large MDE.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Destination on-court net-rating check for movers, corrected for landing-spot quality.
failed_approaches.why: Recorded as underpowered (LIM:low_power_large_MDE, LIM:small_sample), with no sample size or numbers recorded. Dropped from Paper 1 as unanswerable.

evidence_establishes: In an earlier connector-mover study (SF-CHT-057, n=92), a higher pre-move cut share was associated with higher portability of connector function, and drive share with lower portability, with a permutation p of 0.005 as recorded. This is the closest prior evidence to the research question.

Earlier attempts in this project on related questions with smaller samples (SF-APPS-090 with n=19 connectors, SF-APPS-024 with n=44, SF-PAP-029) were recorded as untestable or underpowered, so this project has already found that sample size is the binding constraint for role-transfer questions.
The earlier tests show that a binary or subset-driven result can fail to replicate under a continuous specification, which is a documented analytic-flexibility risk in this project.
evidence_does_not_establish: Nothing retrieved tests cut-heavy versus drive-heavy shapers, or role transfer between regular season and playoffs. The retrieved studies concern connector players who changed teams, so their population and outcome differ from the question as posed.
No retrieved record uses 24 units, so none gives an effect size, variance or power estimate for the present data.

SF-CHT-057 does not show that the effect transfers to shapers, to playoff contexts, or to the 2022-23 to 2025-26 seasons. Its full text was not retrieved, so its covariate handling and cut-share definition are unverified.
The recorded results are not replicated, and the retrieved records do not establish whether the cut/drive classification is reliable for shapers.
own_inferences: The question as posed compares a classification of shapers across 24 units. That is far smaller than the 92-mover sample behind the only supported result, and the power available with 24 units is likely too low to detect a moderate effect (the MDE is probably well above 0.3 in standardized terms, but this is my estimate, not a recorded value).

'Travel better' is probably operationalized as a change in role or function between contexts. Without a pre-specified outcome, the test risks being defined after the data are seen, which the earlier non-replicating binary result illustrates.
A within-season comparison of regular season to playoffs has very different exposure: playoff minutes are much smaller for many units, which increases instability of the shares and the outcome.
Given the 2022-23 to 2025-26 span, rule and playing-style changes could confound any cross-season comparison (DRIFT_NONSTATIONARITY is my inference, not a recorded risk).
uncertainties: The unit definition behind n=24 is not stated (team-seasons, player-seasons, or player-contexts), so the effective sample and independence of units cannot be confirmed.
The retrieved text of SF-CHT-057 is truncated, so the cut-share definition, covariate handling, and reliability of the classification are not verified.
No reliability estimate for the cut/drive shares or for the portability outcome was retrieved.
Playoff data for 2025-26 were only complete from 2026-06-21. The 2026-08-08 date is after that, so the data are complete, but the playoff sample remains small.
Whether the earlier connector finding transfers to shapers is unknown; no record tests this.

historical_effect.explanation: Before retrieval, the question looked testable with the play-by-play data. The retrieved records show that the closest prior test used n=92 connector movers and a pre-specified shuffle and LOO design, and that three related tests with n=19 to n=44 were untestable or underpowered. This makes the n=24 version of the question very unlikely to reach useful power, and shows that a subset or binary result can fail to replicate. The decision therefore moves from a possible test to do_not_proceed as posed, with a reduced design proposed instead.

blocking_constraints.text: With 24 units, a cut-versus-drive contrast will have a power far below 80% for any plausible effect. Earlier related tests with n=19 to n=44 were recorded as untestable or underpowered (SF-APPS-090, SF-APPS-024, SF-PAP-029).
The cut and drive shares are derived from play-type records, and their reliability across seasons and in small playoff samples is not established by any retrieved record.
Playoff possession counts per unit are likely small, so role shares estimated in the playoffs are noisy.

prior_work.summary: SF-CHT-057 reports a supported association between cut share and connector portability in n=92 movers. It is partly relevant because it concerns cut versus drive shares and a portability outcome, but it studies connectors who changed teams, not shapers, and not regular-season-to-playoff transfer. The other three records are untestable or underpowered and address different outcomes. The question as posed is therefore only partly answered, and not for the population or design proposed.

risks.text: n=24 units gives very low power; the MDE is likely much larger than any plausible effect, so a null would be uninformative.
Cut and drive shares from play-type data may be unreliable, especially when computed per unit or in the playoffs.
Playoff exposure is limited, so role shares and outcomes in the playoffs are sparse.
Choosing the most cut-heavy or most portable units for comparison selects on the outcome, inflating apparent transfer.
If portability is defined from the same play-by-play data as the shares, the classification and outcome may be mechanically linked.
Usage, minutes, lineup, teammate and opponent quality, and team context can drive both role shares and transfer outcomes.
Several shares (cut, drive, cut-drive), subgroups and outcomes were examined in the earlier records; the binary-versus-continuous non-replication in SF-APPS-090 shows the flexibility risk.
The 2022-23 to 2025-26 span may include changing play styles and rules, so pooled estimates may mix regimes.
Play-type labels from the NBA stats API may be misclassified, which would bias the cut versus drive split.
The base rate of portability among units is unknown, which affects the interpretation of any hit-rate statistic.

design.estimand: Among shapers, the difference in a pre-registered role-stability or portability outcome between cut-heavy and drive-heavy units, with the cut-share threshold fixed in advance. Reported as a standardized effect with a confidence interval. Not a claim about 'influence' beyond the outcome defined.
design.unit: Unit to be confirmed as team-season or player-season; the 24 units must be defined and independence checked before analysis.
design.sample: The 24 units recorded for the study, drawn from NBA 2022-23 to 2025-26 regular seasons. Playoff contexts are excluded from the primary analysis because of exposure sparsity and are a secondary descriptive check only.
design.power: Not achievable at 24 units for a confirmatory test. Before analysis, compute the MDE at 80% power and report it. If the MDE exceeds the effect size in SF-CHT-057 (standardized rho about 0.27-0.31), the study is descriptive only.
design.controls: Usage rate, minutes, lineup and starter status, teammate quality, opponent quality, and season fixed effects. Reliability of the cut and drive shares is estimated (split-half or across-season) before the main test.
design.falsification: Placebo test on the drive share (which should not carry the same sign if the cut-specific claim holds), label-shuffle permutation (5000 shuffles), and a pre-season placebo window. The result is discounted if the sign flips under a binary versus continuous specification, as in SF-APPS-090.
design.multiplicity: One pre-registered primary contrast (cut-heavy versus drive-heavy). All other shares, subgroups and outcomes are secondary and reported with a correction (Holm or FDR) or as exploratory.
design.decision_rule: Report the primary result as supported only if the pre-registered effect, the permutation test, and the reliability check all pass at the pre-registered alpha, and the MDE is below the effect of interest. Otherwise report as inconclusive or untestable. Do not reinterpret a non-replicating subset result as support.
design.data_version: NBA 2022-23 to 2025-26 regular seasons (complete); 2025-26 playoffs used only from the complete 2026-06-21 snapshot, and only as a secondary check. Freeze the data version and the unit definition before analysis.

research_concepts: role stability across seasons and playoffs
methodological_questions: Can role transferability between regular season and playoffs be tested with n=24 units?
How should cut-heavy versus drive-heavy classification be defined and validated?
Does role-profile reliability and sample size support a group comparison of transfer rates?
What confounders (usage, lineup, opponent quality, minutes) threaten comparisons of role transfer?
args.query: cut-heavy versus drive-heavy shaper roles transfer across seasons and playoffs, play-type derived possession records, n=24 units, NBA 2022-23 to 2025-26

system_prompt:
You are a basketball analytics researcher deciding whether and how a research question should be studied.
You work only from the task statement and the tools listed below. Do not assume facts you have not seen.

The work has two stages, in this order.
Stage 1, retrieval:
1. Read the research objective and the data description.
2. Identify the research concepts and methodological questions the task raises.
3. Retrieve historical evidence by calling retrieve_history.
In stage 1 do not assess the question, predict outcomes or decide. Your only stage-1 reply is the retrieve_history call.
Stage 2, assessment, after the retrieval result is returned:
4. Summarise the relevant historical findings and failed approaches.
5. State what the historical evidence does and does not establish.
6. Assess whether the research question is testable.
7. Identify methodological risks and potential confounders.
8. Make the final research decision.
9. Explain whether and how the historical evidence changed the decision.
The stage-2 output format is given together with the retrieval result.

Evidence rules: keep what a retrieved record states (historical_evidence and failed_approaches, each citing the
identifier of a returned record and its status exactly as recorded) separate from your own inference and from
uncertainty or missing information. Cite only identifiers returned by a tool, and never describe an earlier study that
no tool returned. In some settings retrieval returns no records; then state that no historical evidence was available.

Tools:
- retrieve_history(research_concepts, methodological_questions, query): the prescribed retrieval step. Returns the most relevant consolidated study-family records of earlier research by this project that are available in this setting, with their identifiers; returns an empty list when none are available.
- glossary(): definitions of basketball and project terms used in task statements.
- data_catalog(): the fields available in each per-game data file.
- read_family(id): the complete record of one study family (for example 'FAM:SF-APPA-001').

Protocol: every reply is exactly one JSON object and nothing else.
To call a tool: {"action": "tool", "tool": "<name>", "args": {...}}
To finish (stage 2 only): {"action": "final", "output": <object following the stage-2 schema>}
You may call at most 12 tools; then you must finish. Check that every opening brace has a closing brace.

Risk codes (use only these): SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER, EXPOSURE_SPARSITY, MEASURE_RELIABILITY, RTM_SELECTION, OUTCOME_DERIVED_LABEL, LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD, MECHANICAL_FLOOR, BASE_RATE, CONFOUNDING, LABEL_ERROR, PLACEBO_DEPENDENCE, MULTIPLE_TESTING, IMPLEMENTATION_BUG, DRIFT_NONSTATIONARITY

messages.content:
Research question (as posed on 2026-08-08, in the area of structural roles and influence):
Cut-heavy shapers' roles travel better than drive-heavy ones.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.
- Units available to a study of this question (as recorded): n=24

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.
